title: DfE Article #153: The DfE's New Five to Twelve Study
author: Paul Urry
source: Paul Urry's DfE Decoded newsletter (paulurry68.substack.com), September 6, 2026
summary: A headteacher reviews the UK Department for Education's new 'Five to Twelve' longitudinal study, which will track the same cohort of 8,632 children from Year 1 in 2023/24 through the end of primary school, and argues its early value lies less in any single statistic than in showing how disadvantage, SEND, health, and home circumstances overlap rather than sitting in separate boxes. He highlights specific, concrete figures behind the abstraction of 'disadvantage' -- 10% of households struggling with bills, 10% skipping meals for lack of money, and among FSM-eligible families a quarter cutting meals and 34% unable to afford school essentials -- alongside a striking measurement gap in SEND identification, where only 8% of children were flagged as having special educational needs by both administrative data and parental report, despite 94% of concerned parents saying they had discussed it with school. The piece draws a direct line from disadvantage to self-regulation, noting that 63% of children with SEN sat in the lowest quartile for cognitive self-regulation compared to 20% of children without SEN, and argues this should shift how schools interpret classroom behavior -- not asking 'why isn't this child following the expectation' but 'what does this child continue to need us to teach.' The author closes by naming joined-up thinking as the real leadership lesson: schools structure improvement plans (attendance strategy, SEND strategy, behaviour policy) as though these domains are independent, when the data shows they overlap in the same children, meaning a single child at nine o'clock in the classroom carries poverty, SEND status, sleep deprivation, and self-regulation gaps simultaneously, not as separate initiatives to be addressed one at a time.
points: The SEND identification gap is the report's most striking methodological finding: only 8% of children were flagged as having special educational needs by both administrative records and parental report, despite 12% being recorded administratively and 16% reported by parents -- a mismatch the author connects directly to how identification, conversation, and provision are three distinct things that don't automatically align.

The direct statistical link between disadvantage and self-regulation (63% of children with SEN in the lowest cognitive self-regulation quartile vs. 20% without; 39% vs. 22% for FSM-eligible vs. non-eligible) is used to reframe classroom behavior questions from 'why won't this child follow the expectation' to 'what does this child still need to be taught.'

The essay's central leadership argument is that schools organize improvement plans (attendance strategy, SEND strategy, pupil premium strategy, behaviour policy) as though these domains are independent, when the data shows poverty, SEND, sleep, and self-regulation compound within the same individual children rather than existing as separate initiatives.

Teachers were already predicting Key Stage 2 outcomes for Year 1 children (78% expected to reach the standard in maths, 77% in reading), with the familiar disadvantage gaps present at age five to six -- meaning the study's real long-term value will be tracking whether early teacher predictions prove accurate or whether specific interventions change trajectories.
quotes: This first report looks at 8,632 children who were in Year 1 in 2023/24. And they'll keep coming back to them.
Among families eligible for FSM, a quarter had cut or skipped meals, and 34% had been unable to afford school essentials.

According to the National Pupil Database, 12% of the children were recorded as having SEN. When parents were asked, the figure was 16%. And only 8% of all children were identified as having SEN by both measures. Among parents who had identified SEN or other difficulties, 94% said they had discussed them with school.
Among children with SEN, 63% were in the lowest quartile for cognitive self-regulation, compared with 20% of children without SEN. For FSM-eligible children, it was 39%, compared with 22%.

Teachers were asked whether they thought these Year 1 children would reach the expected standard at the end of Key Stage 2. They predicted that 78% would do so in maths and 77% in reading. And the familiar differences were already there.
Health can affect attendance. None of that is particularly surprising. But schools often organise improvement as though these things exist independently. They don't.
